system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2178-01-03 09:09:00 to 2178-01-07 17:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for worsening shortness of breath and fluid retention, with a plan to undergo right heart catheterization to assess pulmonary pressures. He had gained weight and required 4L of oxygen at night. Due to thrombocytopenia previously linked to Remodulin, dose escalation was not pursued. He was treated with IV diuresis to reduce fluid overload before the procedure. Right heart catheterization revealed improved pulmonary artery systolic pressure at 38 mm Hg, down from 47 mm Hg, with normal filling pressures and preserved cardiac index. His oxygen requirements remained stable. He was discharged home on unchanged medications, including Remodulin at 45 ng/kg/min, furosemide, amiloride, and other home therapies. He was instructed to monitor weight and follow up with specialty care.
problems: Esophageal varices in diseases classified elsewhere, without mention of bleeding
Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma
Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol
Other vasodilators causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

INDICATION: ___ year old man with hep c cirrhosis, portopulmonary hypertension
requiring ___ catheter. 

RADIOLOGISTS: Dr. ___ (resident), Dr. ___ (fellow),
Dr. ___ (attending). Dr ___ was present in the room and monitored
the entire procedure.

ANESTHESIA:  
Moderate sedation was provided by administering divided doses of 200 mcg
fentanyl and 2.5 mg of Versed throughout the total intraservice time of 35
minutes during which patient's hemodynamic parameters were continuously
monitored.
Local anesthesia was provided by 1% lidocaine to the dermis and 1% lidocaine
with epinephrine into the subcutaneous tissues.

RADIATION: time 4.0 min, dose 10 mGy.

PROCEDURE: 
Written informed consent was obtained from the patient after explaining the
procedure, risks, benefits, and alternatives. 
The patient was transported to the angiography suite and placed supine on the
imaging table.  The right neck was prepped and draped in usual sterile
fashion. A preprocedure huddle and timeout was performed per ___ protocol.
After anesthetizing the skin and subcutaneous tissues a micropuncture needle
was inserted into the right internal jugular vein under ultrasound guidance. 
Hard copy ultrasound images were saved for reference.  A 0.018 nitinol wire
was advanced into the superior vena cava.  After additional anesthesia, a
small ___ was made in the skin.  Micropuncture needle was exchanged with
micropuncture sheath.  The inner cannula and nitinol wire were removed.  A
0.035 J-wire was advanced into the right atrium.  Appropriate measurements
were made for skin incision four fingerbreadths below the venotomy site. The
catheter was determined to have a size of 24 cm. The wire was then advanced
into the IVC. 
Attention was now turned to creation of subcutaneous tunnel.  After additional
local anesthesia, a 1-cm skin incision was made.  A 10 ___ tunneled
catheter was passed from the incision to the venotomy site with aid of metal
tunneling device.  The venotomy tract was dilated with 7 and 9 ___
dilators.  Peel-away sheath was passed over the wire.  The wire and inner
cannula were removed and the catheter was passed through the peel-away sheath.
The peel-away sheath was removed while the catheter was pushed into the right
atrium.  This was confirmed with fluoroscopy demonstrating the catheter tip in
the right atrium.  The single lumen withdrew blood and flushed easily.  The
catheter was secured with ___ silk sutures.  Venotomy site was closed with 2
Vicryl subcuticular stitch.  Dry sterile dressings were applied.  No immediate
post-procedure complications were noted.  The patient tolerated the procedure
well.

IMPRESSION:  
Successful placement of tunneled single lumen 24 cm Hickman catheter via a
right internal jugular vein approach.  The tip is located in the right atrium
and the catheter is ready for use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___. I understand your Remodulin catheter came out while you were showering?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. The pump fell off the hook and pulled the line right out. It was out for about three hours before I got to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ve checked a chest X-ray and there’s no sign of a collapsed lung, which is good. Your oxygen levels are stable on 4 liters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But I’ve also had diarrhea for a few days—could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. You mentioned you ate some rancid butter recently. That could explain the diarrhea. We’ll test your stool to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my back pain is still there, but it’s the same as usual—chronic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll manage that with your regular pain meds. Right now, your labs show low white blood cells, potassium, and platelets. We’ll monitor those closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Low white blood cells? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we need to watch. You’ve had low counts before due to your liver disease. But with the fever and diarrhea, we want to rule out infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a fever at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your temperature was normal when you arrived. We’ll keep checking. For now, we’ll restart your Remodulin through a peripheral IV until we can place a new central line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can’t I just go home with the peripheral line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can work short-term, but it’s not safe long-term. We need to place a new tunneled catheter, but not until we’re sure there’s no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely a few days. We’ll wait until you’re afebrile for 48 hours and blood cultures are negative before placing the new line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You spiked a fever last night—101.8. Your white count dropped to 0.7. We’re calling this febrile neutropenia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fever? I felt a little warm. Is it an infection from the catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but your chest ultrasound showed no fluid collection at the site. We’ve started antibiotics—vancomycin and Zosyn—to cover all bases.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Vancomycin? I’ve had a reaction before—red man syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving it slowly and will monitor you closely. We also did a CT scan of your abdomen—no ascites, but your spleen is larger than before, which explains the low platelets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my liver disease is causing the low blood counts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely splenic sequestration. But we’re still checking for other causes. Your stool test came back negative for C. diff and other infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the butter probably just gave me a stomach bug?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our best guess. Blood cultures are still pending, but so far no growth. We’ll keep you on antibiotics for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your fever is gone, and your neutrophil count is starting to rise. Blood cultures are negative. We’re confident you’re not infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I get the new line in now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve scheduled it for tomorrow. You’ll get one unit of platelets first, since your count is still low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the procedure be painful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation—fentanyl and Versed—so you’ll be very relaxed. The line will go into your right internal jugular vein and tunnel under the skin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And it’ll be secure this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll teach you how to anchor the pump properly to avoid another dislodgement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. ___. The procedure went well. You now have a new Hickman catheter in your right chest. The tip is in the right atrium, and it’s working perfectly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel a thing. How soon can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely tomorrow. Your oxygen needs are stable, and your pulmonary pressures are still improved from your last catheterization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My potassium is still low, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s likely due to your diuretics and Remodulin. We’re increasing your magnesium to 800 mg daily and continuing your potassium and calcium supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more blood tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ve set up follow-up with hematology. They’ll check your blood counts and help figure out why they’re chronically low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver transplant evaluation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on the list. Your cirrhosis is stable, and no new issues have come up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh yourself daily. Call if you gain more than three pounds. Watch the catheter site for redness, swelling, or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All the same, except magnesium is now 800 mg daily. Continue your furosemide, amiloride, sildenafil, and Remodulin at 45 ng/kg/min.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need lab work, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—potassium, calcium, magnesium, CBC, and platelets next week. Fax the results to Dr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have pulmonology, hepatology, and hematology visits scheduled. Keep all of them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in clinic soon. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—can I shower with the new line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but cover the site with a waterproof dressing. And make sure the pump is securely hooked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No more accidents.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll provide written instructions before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I’ll follow everything closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Just keep monitoring and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The nurse will bring your discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to being home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you’re set up for success. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last question—should I restart my gabapentin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can resume all your home meds except where we made changes. Gabapentin is fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I was missing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll include it in your discharge list. All set.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted after accidental dislodgement of his tunneled Remodulin catheter while showering. He developed febrile neutropenia on hospital day 2 with a white blood cell count of 0.7 and ANC of 234, likely due to recent gastroenteritis from consuming rancid butter. He was treated with vancomycin and Zosyn for 3 days, remained afebrile after day 3, and blood cultures were negative. A new tunneled central line was placed on hospital day 4 after platelet transfusion and confirmation of no active infection. His portopulmonary hypertension remained stable on Remodulin 45 ng/kg/min and sildenafil, with no change in oxygen requirements. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia were managed with supplementation, and magnesium oxide was increased to 800 mg daily. He was discharged home with outpatient follow-up in hematology, pulmonology, and hepatology, and instructions to monitor weight and catheter site.
